cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T5 answers T4's rehearsal directly; T6 extends the test in reply to T5's sampling objection.
cells.limitation: T3's asymmetry argument (hours cannot be re-earned) is never taken up by the Forecast Skeptic.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T6 adds testing the job itself; T7 turns it into investment versus toll; T8-T9 add finite purpose versus drift.
cells.limitation: T10 mostly recaps; its reversibility point adds little beyond T4.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: Money versus hours (T1-T3) and forecast versus trial (T4-T5, T10) are examined.
cells.limitation: No turn debates sleep, health, family time or driving versus train; these appear only in sections A and E.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T7 and T9 show the Time Accountant reshaped by T6 and T8 while keeping a narrowed position.
cells.limitation: The Forecast Skeptic's view is never reshaped by the others; T10 smooths with 'agree on more'.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D reframes the question into money's purpose, hours' alternative use and the job's own value.
cells.limitation: The remaining hours-versus-money default disagreement is stated in D but not sharpened in T10.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T4 fairly characterises T1-T3 as forecasting from a desk chair before offering an alternative.
cells.limitation: T3 calls commute-fading 'your claim', a stretch of what T2 actually said.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T5 names T4's assumption (a novel trial predicts day two hundred); T6 answers by extending the test.
cells.limitation: T2's challenge to T1 rests on vividness alone; nobody tests whether commutes actually fade.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: T1's fifteen hours a week checks out: 90 min x 2 x 5 days.
cells.limitation: T1 never computes the raise per extra hour; section E asserts the gain is 'modest' without numbers.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T3 'I'd go further than Burkeman here' separates the speaker's view from the source.
cells.limitation: Section A and T1 treat all fifteen hours as added though current commute is listed unknown.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T9 concedes T8's point yet keeps a narrowed claim: hours vote before salary.
cells.limitation: T3's 'benefit of the doubt' argument goes unanswered rather than conceded or rebutted.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern
cells.example: Section A names the decisive uncertainty: whether the pay buys something worth fifteen weekly hours.
cells.limitation: Why the user sought or is tempted by this offer is only touched in D's reflection.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T1 converts 90 minutes each way into fifteen weekly hours, a second unpaid job.
cells.limitation: T1 uses a 'hypothetical salary'; the computable raise per extra hour is never stated.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: T9 and D keep the Accountant's hours-first preference marked as a speaker view, not the user's.
cells.limitation: The user stated no priorities; the debate rarely asks which the user holds until section D.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: Section E weighs fares, fuel, tax, evenings, sleep, family and health time.
cells.limitation: Section A assumes the full three hours are added despite current commute being unknown.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on money's purpose, remote days, train versus car and job sameness.
cells.limitation: Current commute length, listed unknown in A, never becomes a branch.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: D asks whether the user wants the job without the raise, or the money without the job.
cells.limitation: Dissatisfaction with the current job as a possible motive is never offered.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T2 exposes the focusing illusion; T8 questions the assumption that growth will materialise.
cells.limitation: The assumption that the commute is fixed (no relocation, no hybrid) is only partly surfaced in T6.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: T7 and T9 set growth, finite financial goals and free hours against each other.
cells.limitation: What the freed hours currently hold for the user is never asked inside the debate.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T9 names drift; T8 notes excitement inflating growth.
cells.limitation: No turn raises obligation, family expectation, fear of missing out or habit behind staying.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: D's two-sided question and T9's sacrifice-versus-drift distinction are offered for the user to apply.
cells.limitation: Turns address the minds more than the user; few distinctions are posed as user questions.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options
cells.example: Accept, stay, negotiate remote days (T6), trial (T4) and time-limited acceptance (T9) appear.
cells.limitation: Moving closer or negotiating pay to offset commute costs is never raised.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
cells.example: T7 frames hours as investment when growth is real, toll when work is the same.
cells.limitation: Costs to sleep, health and relationships appear only as a list in section E.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: remote days or a train ride make the offer better; job sameness favours staying.
cells.limitation: T8-T9's 'two years' is not drawn from user facts; no raise-per-hour threshold computed.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: Section A names money-versus-hours as the decisive uncertainty among several unknowns.
cells.limitation: Consequential unknowns are not ranked against minor ones in section E.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps
cells.example: Section E: ride at rush hour, ask employees about home days, ask for a trial, compute hourly gain.
cells.limitation: T6's week-long shadowing is heavy for a candidate weighing an offer.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T2 'Hours and dollars aren't the same currency' states the idea plainly.
cells.limitation: T1's divide-a-hypothetical-salary instruction is hard to follow without a number.

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T8 'a challenge for both of you' and T9 'I'll concede that' point clearly at T6-T8.
cells.limitation: T3 'which is your claim' points at T2 for a claim T2 only implied.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Ten turns, all within range per DETERMINISTIC CHECKS, each carrying one move.
cells.limitation: Sections D and E are dense single paragraphs after an evenly paced debate.

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
cells.example: Stances stay distinct; T7 and T9 mark explicit position changes.
cells.limitation: Near-identical turn lengths and one calm register across all three minds, T1-T10.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: T10's recap serves to isolate the one remaining disagreement.
cells.limitation: Section D partly repeats T9-T10 before the reflection question.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
cells.example: T1: fifteen hours is 'a second part-time job that pays nothing'.
cells.limitation: Stakes stay abstract; no turn pictures a concrete evening or relationship lost.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals
cells.example: T9's concession is traced to T8's debt-and-savings argument and named as such.
cells.limitation: Both reversals (T7, T9) are mild and polite; none surprises.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice
cells.example: T4 'arguing from a desk chair' gives the Experimenter some edge.
cells.limitation: All three minds share one measured register; little individual flavour.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T7 investment versus toll; T9 bargain versus drift; T5 'Day two hundred'.
cells.limitation: No humour or extended example; images are brief phrases.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
cells.example: T8's challenge to both minds lifts the middle of the debate.
cells.limitation: Uniform length and even tone T1-T10 give little emotional movement.

strengths: T6-T9 build new distinctions in sequence: job versus commute, investment versus toll, finite sacrifice versus drift.
T9's concession is caused by T8's argument and keeps a narrowed position rather than collapsing.
Section E turns unknowns into observable conditions and proportionate steps like a rush-hour trial ride.
weaknesses: No turn debates sleep, health, family time or driving versus train; they appear only in sections A and E.
T1 leaves the raise per extra hour uncomputed although the user's percentages allow it.
All three minds share one register and near-identical turn lengths, flattening voice and rhythm.

symptoms.observed: Health, sleep, family time and travel mode never debated in any turn.
symptoms.evidence: Money is easy to count; hours are what you actually spend.

symptoms.observed: Raise per extra commuting hour never computed from the user's 25% and 90 minutes.
symptoms.evidence: Take a 25% raise on a hypothetical salary

symptoms.observed: No obligation, family expectation or habit offered as a pressure on either choice.
symptoms.evidence: Commuting indefinitely because the raise looked bigger than the hours

symptoms.observed: Every turn similar length and calm tone; no shift in intensity.
symptoms.evidence: So we agree on more than we admit.

symptoms.observed: Treats commute adaptation as symmetrical with raise adaptation without support.
symptoms.evidence: If the raise will fade into the background, the commute might too

findings.description: T1 says the raise 'may shrink' without computing it; E calls the gain 'modest' unsupported. Check, assuming a 40-hour week and no current commute: extra pay 0.25S over 15 extra hours/week = S/60 per hour versus S/40 now, about two-thirds of the current hourly rate pre-tax; overall hourly 1.25S/55 versus S/40, about 9% lower.
Section A lists current commute as unknown yet treats all fifteen weekly hours as added.
T3 suggests the commute may fade like the raise; Kahneman's day-reconstruction work rated commuting among the least pleasant activities, and commutes are often cited as resisting adaptation.
Paraphrase that Burkeman warns about optimising a commute specifically could not be confirmed; general anti-optimisation theme fits the book.

rubric_fit_notes: The user supplied only two facts, so personal-relevance cells rest mainly on how unknowns were handled.
The Kahneman adaptation concern relies on evaluator memory and is reported as suspected.
question_type_note: As a decision question, every cell was read as written, with criterion 5 judged on options, conditions and next steps for accepting or declining the offer.
